transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Well, to be honest, what brings me in is... I just cannot keep my mind on one single thing anymore. I mean, I've been a carpenter for a long time, and you'd think I'd be used to a busy shop by now, but lately it's just out of control. 

I'll be right in the middle of measuring a piece of wood or trying to focus on cutting a joint, and just one saw starting up across the room—maybe somebody firing up the miter saw or the table saw—and my attention is completely gone. Or I'll be sitting down trying to look at some plans, and somebody simply walks past the office window. They don't even say anything, they just walk past, and I'm totally derailed. I stop what I'm doing to watch them or wonder what they're doing. 

And sometimes it's not even something happening around me, you know? I'll just be working and a random thought about a completely different job will pop into my head—like wondering if the hinges for the Miller house ever got delivered—and that one thought will pull me completely off what I’m doing right then and there. Next thing I know, I've walked away from my workbench, I'm wandering around looking for a shipping invoice for a totally different project, and then... well, the whole day just gets away from me. I look at the clock and it's quitting time, and I realize I never finished that first thing I started at eight in the morning. It's just happening every single day now, and it's so frustrating because I'll have all these good intentions when I walk in the door, but the second there's a noise or a thought, I'm just completely off track.
When did you first start noticing these difficulties with staying focused? Were they present when you were a child, or did they start more recently?

Oh, gosh, no, it is definitely not a recent thing. Not at all. If I really think back on it... I mean, way back, long before I even hit junior high, it was happening. I must have been, oh, maybe nine or ten? Definitely before I was twelve, anyway. I remember being in Mrs. Gable's class in the fourth grade, and then Mr. Henderson in fifth, and it was the exact same story every single year at those parent-teacher conferences. My mother would come home and sit me down at the kitchen table—it was this old yellow formica table, I can still picture it perfectly—and she would just sigh and shake her head. 

The teachers were always telling her that I was a bright girl, but that I was just so careless. And it was true, I guess. I was always, always losing my homework. I would do it at home, or at least I thought I did it, and then it would just vanish somewhere between my backpack and the teacher's desk. Or they would give us instructions for an assignment, you know, step one, step two, and by the time they got to step three I had completely forgotten what they even said for step one. 

And the windows... the windows were my absolute downfall. I would be supposed to be doing my seatwork, just a simple worksheet of math problems or spelling words, and I would catch sight of a bird outside, or the janitor raking leaves, or literally just the clouds moving. Next thing I knew, twenty minutes had gone by, my paper was completely blank, and I was just staring out the glass instead of finishing my work. It drove my mother absolutely crazy. They just could not understand why I could not just sit and finish a simple worksheet like all the other kids. 

So, yeah, it has been happening my whole life, really. I just... I guess I thought I would outgrow it, you know? You get older, you get a job, you think you can just force yourself to pay attention, but even back then in grade school, it was exactly like it is now in the woodshop. I would just sit there looking out at the playground and... well, anyway, I guess that answers your question about whether it was happening back then. I just never really put it all together until lately when the shop got so bad.
